blocks.prompt: The Dinosaur That Turned to Stone
blocks.text: A fossil is a very old thing that turned into stone. Here is how one dinosaur got inside this rock. The dinosaur died near a river. Sand and mud washed over it fast. That kept it safe. Its skin and its insides went away. Its hard bones stayed. Water dripped down into the bones. The water carried tiny bits of rock. The rock bits filled every little hole in the bones. That took a long, long time. Now the bones are stone. Someone cracked the rock open and saw the dinosaur looking back.

blocks.prompt: The Rock That Kept a Dinosaur
blocks.text: Bones do not usually last. When an animal dies, most of it gets eaten or rots away, and after a few years there is nothing left to find. A fossil happens when something interrupts that. Picture a dinosaur that dies on a riverbank. Before anything can scatter the body, a flood buries it under sand and mud. Now the bones are sealed away from the air and from hungry animals. More mud piles on top, year after year, until the weight presses the mud into solid rock. Water still trickles through that rock. It carries minerals, which are tiny bits of stone too small to see. The water seeps into the bones, because bone is full of holes like a sponge. In each hole, the minerals settle and harden. Little by little, the bone fills with stone. It keeps its exact shape. That is why a fossil bone is cold and heavy to lift. It is rock now. Almost no animal gets this lucky. For every dinosaur that became a fossil, millions simply vanished.

blocks.prompt: Read the passage, then work through each part.

notes: Latin fossilis: dug up

blocks.prompt: Buried Fast, Found Slowly
blocks.text: Most living things leave nothing behind. A body on open ground is picked apart by scavengers, broken down by bacteria, and scattered by wind and rain. Fossils exist only because of accidents that stop that process. The accident is usually burial. A dinosaur that drowns in a flood, sinks into a swamp, or gets covered by a collapsing riverbank is sealed away from the air and from anything that wants to eat it. Soft parts still decay. The hard parts, bones and teeth, stay put. Sediment keeps piling up above them, and the weight squeezes the loose sand and mud into sedimentary rock. Then the slow part begins. Groundwater trickles through the rock, carrying dissolved minerals such as silica and calcite. Bone is porous, full of tiny channels that once carried blood. The mineral-rich water enters those channels and crystals grow inside them. This is called permineralization. The original bone is not replaced so much as filled, like pouring cement into a sponge and letting it set. The result is a copy in stone, accurate down to the shape of a tooth root. Finding one takes one more accident. A fossil buried under a mile of rock is useless to us. Erosion has to strip that rock away and bring the bone back to the surface, where somebody walking past has to notice it before wind and rain destroy it. That is why fossil hunters search cliffs, quarries, and badlands: places where the ground is being peeled open.

blocks.prompt: Reading the Rock
blocks.text: A fossil is not just an old bone. It is a piece of evidence, and evidence has to be read. Start with where it was found. Sedimentary rock forms in layers, each one settling on top of the last, so in ground that has not been folded or flipped over, the deeper layers are older. Nicolas Steno worked that out in 1669, and it still holds. A fossil's layer is its address in time. To turn that address into a number, geologists look for ash beds from ancient eruptions squeezed between the layers. The minerals in ash contain unstable atoms that break down into other atoms at a known, unchanging rate, so measuring what is left gives an age. Carbon dating is useless here. It expires after about fifty thousand years, and the youngest dinosaur bone is more than a thousand times older than that. Some fossils are not body parts at all. A footprint is a fossil. So is a burrow, an egg, a nest, a row of tooth marks, and dung, which paleontologists call a coprolite. These are trace fossils, and they record behavior rather than anatomy. A skeleton tells you how an animal was built. A trackway tells you how fast it walked, whether it dragged its tail, and whether it traveled alone or in a group. One coprolite dug out of Saskatchewan was packed with crushed bone, which showed that Tyrannosaurus did not delicately strip its prey. It shattered the skeleton and swallowed the pieces. Certain species are useful for a different reason. Ammonites and trilobites were widespread and short-lived, so a layer holding one can be matched to a layer on the far side of the world holding the same one. Geologists call these index fossils and use them like date stamps. The rock, in other words, keeps records. The hard part is learning to read the handwriting.

blocks.prompt: Read the passage, then work through each part.

notes: Latin fossilis: dug up
Permineralization builds a stone replica of bone
Thin slices of dinosaur bone show growth rings
Lagerstätte: a site where soft tissue survived
Melanosomes can reveal a dinosaur's color
Mary Anning found Britain's first pterosaur, in 1828

blocks.prompt: The Fossil Record Is a Ruin, Not a Library
blocks.text: Every dinosaur you have ever seen in a museum arrived there through a filter, and the filter threw away almost everything. Consider what has to happen. An animal must die in the right place: a floodplain, a lakebed, a river delta, somewhere sediment is actively piling up. It must be buried quickly, before scavengers scatter it and before oxygen and bacteria finish their work. It must then sit undisturbed for millions of years while the mud around it hardens into rock and mineral-laden groundwater seeps into its bones, growing crystals in the hollow channels that once carried blood. That process is called permineralization, and it produces a replica so faithful that a thin slice of dinosaur bone under a microscope still shows growth rings, like a tree stump. Finally the rock must be lifted and stripped back by erosion at exactly the right moment. Too early, and the fossil weathers to dust before anyone is born to see it. Too late, and it stays buried forever. Then a human being has to walk past and look down. The filter is not neutral. It favors animals with hard parts, so shells and teeth are everywhere while jellyfish and worms are nearly invisible. It favors animals that lived in lowlands near water, and discards those that lived in mountains, where rock is worn away instead of piling up. It favors the common over the rare, and the large over the small. The fossil record is not a library of the past. It is a ruin, and we are reading the few pages the fire missed. Now and then the filter slips. At a handful of sites, conditions were so still and so poor in oxygen that soft tissue survived. Shales in northeastern China have yielded dinosaurs with feathers pressed flat into the rock, and inside those feathers, microscopic structures called melanosomes whose shapes match the ones that produce particular colors in living birds. Researchers have used them to reconstruct the plumage of animals nobody has ever seen alive. In Alberta, a mine worker's shovel struck an armored nodosaur that had drifted out to sea and been buried there, preserved in three dimensions, skin and scales and gut contents intact, still carrying traces of reddish-brown pigment shaded lighter underneath. That pattern is called countershading, and it is used today by small animals that get hunted from above. Sites this generous are rare enough to have their own name: geologists borrowed the German word Lagerstätten, meaning storage places. The person who taught the world to take this evidence seriously had no formal schooling. Mary Anning began collecting fossils as a child on the crumbling cliffs of Lyme Regis, on the English coast, and sold them to support her family after her father died in debt. She was about twelve when the first ichthyosaur skeleton that London scientists had ever properly examined came out of that rock. She went on to find the first two plesiosaurs known to science and the first pterosaur found in Britain, and she worked out that the strange stones scattered through the cliffs were fossilized dung, still full of the bones of whatever the animal had eaten. Geologists traveled down from London to buy her specimens and ask her opinion, then published papers on them and left her name out. She could not join the Geological Society, which did not admit women, and she died at forty-seven having never been made a member of the community she supplied. The cliffs she worked are still producing fossils. The Society admitted its first woman in 1904, fifty-seven years after Anning was gone.
